name: chacha20poly1305-simd
workload: AEAD seal (encrypt_in_place_detached), 16-byte AAD, in-place, across message sizes from 16 B to ≥16 KiB
claimed_speedup: 2.0-3.1x faster than OpenSSL 4.1.0-dev at tiny sizes (16-256B), 1.3-1.9x at mid sizes (512B-1KiB), 1.0-1.1x at large sizes (>=4KiB); also 1.7-6.2x vs RustCrypto chacha20poly1305 0.11 (same ISA tier) and 0.8-1.4x vs aws-lc-rs depending on size
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.100-nightly, cargo bench --release; OpenSSL 4.1.0-dev static build with runtime auto-dispatch (AVX-512 ChaCha + AVX-512 IFMA Poly1305 on this CPU); bench driver perf/openssl_bench.c linked in repo
tradeoffs: Disclaimer in README: developed with AI assistance and has not undergone a security audit; pure Rust with hand-written AVX-512/AVX2/SSE2/NEON backends and runtime CPU dispatch
caveats: Very new project (created Aug 2026), no independent audit or third-party verification of the benchmark; OpenSSL comparison used an OpenSSL 4.1.0-dev pre-release build rather than a stable release

name: hardware-rust-crypto
workload: AES-256-GCM allocation-free encrypt/decrypt (encrypt_to/decrypt_to), Criterion benchmarks over sizes 16B-16KiB
claimed_speedup: Beats ring at every size 16B-16KiB (e.g. 1.77us vs 2.38us at 16KiB encrypt: 8.64 vs 6.41 GiB/s); 14x-43x faster than an unmodified default-build RustCrypto aes-gcm 0.10, and 3.4x-5.0x faster than RustCrypto built with its ARMv8 hardware cfgs enabled
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.96.0, cargo bench (Criterion, default release build); RustCrypto 'armv8 cfgs' variant built with RUSTFLAGS="--cfg aes_armv8 --cfg polyval_armv8"
tradeoffs: AES-256-only (no AES-128), hardware-instruction-only design (no software fallback, so it hard-fails on CPUs lacking AES-NI/ARMv8 crypto extensions); extensively formally verified (Kani, SAW, crux-mir, F*, Z3) as its other main selling point besides speed
caveats: Single-run laptop benchmark; author explicitly states +/-10% run-to-run variance at sub-microsecond sizes and says to read results as 'tie/win/lose, not exact ratios' and to re-run on target Linux x86_64 hardware before integration decisions; project has only 1 GitHub star

name: aegis (rust-aegis)
workload: AEAD encryption throughput chart at 16 KB messages (separate 64 KB chart for MAC-only)
claimed_speedup: On AMD Zen 4 (turbo disabled): AEGIS128L 208.44 Gb/s vs AES-128-GCM(BoringSSL) 50.83 Gb/s (~4.1x) and vs AES-256-GCM(BoringSSL) 47.68 Gb/s (~4.4x); AEGIS128X4 521.36 Gb/s (~10.9x vs AES-256-GCM/BoringSSL) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: clang recommended over gcc; CC="clang -O3 -march=native"; cargo bench / cargo-zigbuild bench; BoringSSL included via --features boring
hardware: AMD Zen 4 (turbo boost disabled); also charted on Apple M1 (MacBook Pro)
tradeoffs: AEGIS is a newer, non-NIST AES-based AEAD (CAESAR/IETF draft); needs AES-NI/ARM crypto extensions for its speed, falling back to a bundled softaes implementation otherwise; the crate vendors the C libaegis sources internally
caveats: Exact numbers are embedded only as a PNG chart in the README (read off the chart here, not machine-parsed text); comparison target is BoringSSL, not OpenSSL directly, so baseline_in_list=false; the vendored C backend derives from the separately-excluded aegis-aead/libaegis project

name: HiAE (libhiae)
workload: AEAD encryption with associated data and tag, 64 KB messages, 4096-byte-aligned buffers
claimed_speedup: On Apple M5 Max: HiAE 266.7 Gbps vs AES-128-GCM(OpenSSL 3.6.4) 70.8 Gbps AEAD encryption (~3.77x, derived from page data). The associated peer-reviewed-style paper (ePrint 2025/377) separately reports HiAE exceeding 340 Gbps on x86 and 180 Gbps on ARM vs OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM baseline across 14 CPUs, e.g. AMD Ryzen 9 7950X AEAD encryption 269.01 Gbps vs AES-256-GCM 84.09 Gbps (~3.2x, derived from paper Table 10)
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 21.0.0 on macOS 26 for the M5 Max run, -O3 -march=native/-mcpu=native; the paper's x86 server results used GCC 11.4 -O3 on Ubuntu 22.04
hardware: Apple M5 Max (macOS 26); paper additionally covers AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, Intel Xeon W9-3495X, and 11 other CPUs (Table 9)
tradeoffs: Newer, non-standardized AES-based AEAD tied to an individual IETF CFRG draft (draft-pham-cfrg-hiae) and ePrint 2025/377; best performance needs clang/zig cc rather than gcc; HiAEx2/HiAEx4 variants are explicitly experimental benchmarking-only, not part of the spec
caveats: The cleanest textual benchmark source (hiae-aead/benchmarks) has no LICENSE file of its own (unrelated to libhiae's separate MIT license); the ePrint paper is a preprint tied to an individual IETF draft, not yet published at a peer-reviewed venue
found_via: 'Known Implementations' table in hiae-aead/draft-pham-hiae README, reached from crates.io q=aes-ni search results

name: ROCCA-S (rust-rocca-s)
workload: AEAD encryption at 64 KB messages, per the hiae-aead/benchmarks cross-cipher shootout
claimed_speedup: ROCCA-S 208.1 Gbps (Apple M5 Max) / 174.6 Gbps (AMD Ryzen 7 7700, Zen4) AEAD encryption vs AES-128-GCM(OpenSSL) 70.8 Gbps on the M5 Max run (~2.9x, derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: clang 21.1.8 (Zen4 run) / Apple clang 21.0.0 (M5 Max run), -O3 -march=native (-mcpu=native on ARM); OpenSSL 3.5.5 (Zen4) / 3.6.4 (M5 Max)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen4, boost disabled, performance governor); Apple M5 Max (macOS 26)
tradeoffs: ROCCA-S is a newer, non-standardized AES-based AEAD; its published speed depends on AES-NI/ARM crypto extensions
caveats: The hiae-aead/benchmarks shootout measures its own vendored C reference implementation of ROCCA-S (rocca-s.c), not literally the jedisct1/rust-rocca-s crate; cited here as evidence for the ROCCA-S algorithm/family rather than this exact binary. rust-rocca-s itself has no LICENSE file (unclear license, hence usability=reference)
found_via: gh api graphql code search 'Rocca-S authenticated encryption', cross-referenced with the hiae-aead/benchmarks shootout
